issues.issue: The grant covers the property "including, but not limited to, fixtures, existing improvements, and appurtenant structures," a catch-all that leaves the licensed subject matter unbounded beyond the enumerated items. Because Exhibit A itself is also framed as "include, but is not limited to," nothing in the instrument fixes the outer edge of what was licensed.

It is unclear whether "the Premises will be declared surplus property and deemed not needed for public use by the Director of Finance" states an existing fact, a condition precedent to the license, or a promise of future municipal action. "Economic development purposes" is likewise given no boundary.

"Hardrives intends to utilize the Premises for..." is a statement of intention, so it is ambiguous whether this sentence is a binding use covenant limiting occupancy or merely recites expected use. The added phrase "other similar products" gives the permitted-use list no determinate limit.

The blanket permission to store and operate "all equipment, personal property, and supplies necessary for said purposes" cannot easily be squared with Section 7.D, which requires Hardrives to take all precautions against the creation, use, or storage of any hazardous material on the Premises. Asphalt-production supplies and fuels fall on both sides of the two provisions.

A rental fee of "$1.00 per year" sits awkwardly with Section 5, under which the Agreement runs only one year or until title passes, so it is unclear whether more than a single payment is ever owed. Section 4 nonetheless keys default to "annual payments."

The cure/default period is written as "thirty (80) days," a numeral-versus-words discrepancy that changes the length of the period a court would have to fix. Ohio's usual rule prefers the written words, but the figure is squarely inconsistent.

The clause runs the default period from "the date payment is due," but Section 3 fixes no due date for the $1.00 annual rental anywhere in the Agreement. The trigger for default therefore depends on a term the instrument never supplies.

"Upon written notice by the City, Hardrives shall have ten (10) days, within which to cure" does not say whether written notice is a condition precedent to any declaration of default or merely starts the cure clock. It also leaves unclear how this ten-day period relates to the thirty-day grace period in the preceding sentence.

The stray colon in "within that ten (10) day period: following notice from the City" detaches the notice requirement from the cure period, so the sentence can be read either as requiring notice before the period runs or as requiring a second notice after it. The punctuation changes when the breach is deemed to occur.

The disjunctive "or" between a one-year term and continuation "until the date that title to the Premises is conveyed" leaves it indeterminate whether the license ends at the earlier or the later of those events, and what happens if no Development Agreement is executed by December 31, 1999. Nothing else in the instrument resolves which branch controls.

The representation is given "as of the date hereof, and on the date of the execution, delivery, and performance of this Agreement," which purports to speak as of future and open-ended dates. It is also unclear whether authorization of "the Board of Control" by "the City Council" is asserted as accomplished or assumed.

The warranty of "full authority to license the use of the Premises" is difficult to square with Section 2, which contemplates that the Premises must still "be declared surplus property and deemed not needed for public use by the Director of Finance." If that declaration had not occurred, the City's stated authority and the Section 2 condition point in opposite directions.

The exception for "any and all unrecorded easements identified by the City prior to the execution of this Agreement" points to an identification that is nowhere attached, listed, or otherwise fixed in the instrument. Whether the Premises are "clear of all liens and claims" therefore turns on an undefined external set.

"Affecting the Premises" is unbounded and does not say whether it reaches the site-wide RCRA/CERCLA listing described in the Exhibit B assessment. It is also unclear whether that qualifier limits the whole sentence or only the enumerated governmental orders.

"Threatened" proceedings that "may affect the Premises" is an open-ended standard with no knowledge qualifier and no measure of likelihood or materiality. A court would have to supply the boundary of what merely "may" affect the property.

"All easements and right of ways, as may be necessary to have access to, and utilization of, the Premises" supplies no measure of necessity and does not identify the easements granted. Whether a given access route is "necessary" is left entirely at large.

The trailing qualifier "in violation of any applicable environmental laws or regulations" is placed after the Exhibit B exception, leaving it unclear whether the City warranted the absence of any hazardous or toxic materials at all or only of materials present in violation of law. The whole scope of the environmental warranty turns on that misplaced modifier.

The carve-out is measured by the Environmental Site Assessment attached as Exhibit B, but that report describes a "Parcel No. 3" of 5.44 acres, whereas Exhibit A's Parcel No. 3 is a 58.086-acre tract. What conditions are excepted from the warranty cannot be determined without reconciling the two exhibits.

The representation that "no 'clean-up' of the Premises has occurred pursuant to any applicable federal or state environmental laws or regulations" is in tension with the Exhibit B assessment, which states that RCRA-regulated portions of the study area were closed in 1985 to 1988 in accordance with Ohio EPA and U.S. EPA protocols. Whether that closure was a "clean-up" within this sentence is left to be construed.
